R05-F-01: Few ideas in economics are cited as often, or misunderstood as thoroughly, as comparative advantage. In everyday commentary trade is described as a contest: a country wins when it is better at making things than its rivals and loses when they overtake it. On this view a nation that is less productive than its neighbours in every industry would have nothing to sell and would be wise to close its borders. The principle of comparative advantage was formulated precisely to show why this conclusion does not follow, and the fact that the conclusion is still drawn suggests that the principle is more often invoked than understood. The core insight concerns opportunity cost rather than absolute ability. Consider a hypothetical lawyer who types faster than any secretary she could hire. It does not follow that she should do her own typing, because every hour spent at the keyboard is an hour withdrawn from legal work that earns far more. The secretary, though slower at typing, gives up much less by doing it. Both are better off when each concentrates on the task in which his or her relative sacrifice is smallest and they exchange the results. The same reasoning applies to countries. What determines the pattern of trade is not which country is best at producing a good, but which country forgoes the least of other goods in producing it, and every country, however unproductive overall, has some activity in which that sacrifice is comparatively low. Two consequences follow that sit uneasily with the language of contest. First, gains from trade do not require one party to lose: the lawyer and the secretary both gain, and so do a rich and a poor economy that trade on the basis of their differing costs. Second, a country cannot have a comparative advantage in everything, since being relatively better at one activity means, by definition, being relatively worse at another. A government that promises to make its nation competitive in every industry is therefore promising something that is not merely difficult but incoherent. None of this implies that the critics of open trade have nothing to say. The textbook argument compares two settled states and is silent about the passage between them; workers who lose their jobs when an industry contracts do not costlessly reappear in the industry that expands, and the losses can be concentrated in particular towns for a generation. Comparative advantage can also shift over time as skills and capital accumulate, which is why some economists defend temporary support for new industries. These are serious objections, but they are objections to the timing and distribution of the gains, not to the logic of opportunity cost. They do not restore the image of trade as a race in which one runner's progress is another's defeat.
R05-F-02: Special economic zones are usually defended with a simple argument. Where a country's regulations, infrastructure or courts are too poor to attract investors, it may be impossible to repair them everywhere at once; it is easier to draw a boundary around a small area, supply it with reliable power, quick customs clearance and predictable rules, and invite firms to set up inside. The zone becomes a place where the business environment the country cannot yet afford for itself is provided in miniature. Inside the fence, so the thinking goes, investors will find conditions that would take a generation to create outside it. The reasoning is persuasive within its limits, and it explains why so many governments have tried the experiment. But it also contains the seed of a common failure. A zone designed to protect investors from the surrounding economy can succeed too well. Firms import their components free of duty, assemble them with local labour and export the finished product, while buying almost nothing from domestic suppliers and teaching them nothing. Export figures rise, and an observer counting shipments would call the zone a triumph. Yet the economy outside the fence may be little changed, apart from the wages paid to workers who commute in, and those wages often reflect the kind of routine assembly that is easiest to move elsewhere when costs rise. What distinguishes the zones that have mattered is not the generosity of their tax holidays but the degree to which they leak. In the more instructive cases, local firms learned to supply the foreign plants, managers trained inside the zone left to start businesses outside it, and, most important, rules first tried within the boundary were later extended across the country once they had shown that they worked. The zone, on this view, is less an enclave than a laboratory, and a laboratory whose findings never leave the building has failed at its central task, whatever it produces. It would be naive to conclude that governments should simply abolish the boundary and expect the benefits to spread. The isolation of a zone is often what makes it politically possible in the first place, since it lets reformers try new rules without confronting at once every interest that benefits from the old ones. The point is that isolation should be treated as a starting condition to be outgrown, not as the design itself. A zone that is still, after decades, an island of efficiency in an unchanged sea is evidence less of success than of a reform that stalled.
R05-F-03: As tariffs have fallen over the past several decades, attention in trade disputes has shifted to a less visible kind of obstacle: the technical standards a product must meet before it can be sold. Rules on labelling, safety testing, permitted additives and packaging are written for reasons that sound unimpeachable, and many of them are exactly what they claim to be. But a rule can protect consumers and domestic producers at the same time, and it is not always easy to say which purpose is doing the work. The usual complaint is that standards are protectionism by other means, and examples are easy to imagine. Suppose a country requires that cheese be aged in wooden barrels of a particular kind, a method its own dairies have used for generations, while foreign producers age theirs in steel vessels that yield a product no less safe. The rule says nothing explicit about origin, and its authors need never mention foreign cheese at all, yet its effect is almost that of a ban on imports. A tariff of this severity would be denounced at once; dressed as a quality rule, it may pass unnoticed for years. It does not follow, however, that every standard which burdens importers is suspect. Almost any rule imposes costs on foreign firms, if only because they must learn it, and societies differ honestly in the risks they will tolerate. One country may accept a pesticide residue that another refuses, not because its farmers lobbied but because its citizens weigh the balance between price and caution differently. To treat all such divergence as disguised protection would be to deny countries the right to set their own levels of acceptable risk, which is a large part of what self-government means. The more useful test is therefore not whether a standard falls harder on foreigners, but whether its burden is necessary to the purpose it states. A rule that specifies an outcome, such as a maximum level of bacteria, leaves producers free to reach it by any method and so admits anyone who can meet it. A rule that specifies a method, when other methods would achieve the same outcome, deserves closer scrutiny, because the extra cost it imposes buys no additional safety. The distinction will not settle every dispute; outcomes can be hard to measure, and a method is sometimes prescribed precisely because checking the outcome is impractical. But it shifts the argument from motives, which are hard to prove, to fit, which can at least be examined.
R05-F-04: For a generation, the managers of manufacturing firms were taught to regard inventory as waste. Parts sitting in a warehouse tie up money, take up space and conceal problems that a tighter system would expose, so the ideal was to have each component arrive just as it was needed, often from a single supplier chosen because it was the cheapest or the best. Applied across borders, this logic produced supply chains of remarkable length and precision, in which a product might cross several frontiers as it was assembled, with little stock held at any stage. The gains were real, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them in hindsight. Lower costs reached consumers as lower prices, and firms in poorer countries gained access to markets they could not otherwise have entered. But a system tuned to perform well under normal conditions can perform very badly under abnormal ones. When a single factory, port or region on which many chains depend is shut by a fire, a flood or a closed border, there is no slack anywhere to absorb the shock, and the shortage of one cheap part can halt the assembly of goods worth thousands of times as much. A popular response is to call for production to be brought home. The instinct is understandable, but as a remedy for fragility it is oddly chosen. A chain that depends on one domestic plant is no less exposed to a single fire or flood than one that depends on a single foreign plant; it has merely moved its point of failure to a place that feels more familiar. What protects against disruption is not proximity but redundancy: more than one supplier for critical parts, suppliers in places unlikely to suffer the same shock at the same time, and stocks large enough to bridge an interruption. Redundancy, however, costs money, which is precisely why lean systems eliminated it. A firm deciding how much spare capacity to keep weighs the expense against its own expected losses from a disruption, but some of the losses fall on others: on patients who cannot obtain a medicine, on other firms whose lines stop, on workers sent home without pay. Because these costs do not appear in the firm's accounts, it will tend to hold less insurance than would be sensible for the economy as a whole. The real question, then, is not where things are made but who pays for the resilience that markets left to themselves will tend to supply too sparingly.
R05-F-05: When a country lowers its barriers to imports, the gains and the losses arrive in very different forms. The gains are spread thinly across millions of households, each of which pays a little less for clothing, appliances or food, usually without noticing why. The losses fall heavily on a few: the workers of a particular mill, the shops that depended on their wages, the town whose tax base was the mill. A small saving that nobody notices is politically weightless; a closed factory is a photograph on the front page. Those who lose know exactly what they have lost and whom to blame, while those who gain rarely connect their small savings to a decision taken in a distant ministry. It is not surprising that the politics of trade so often seems out of proportion to its economics. Economists have a standard reply. Because the total gains exceed the total losses, the winners could in principle compensate the losers and still come out ahead, so that everyone ends up better off. The argument is correct as arithmetic, and it is the foundation of the case that open trade raises national welfare. But the word that carries the weight is 'could'. A compensation that is possible but never paid is no comfort to the people who bore the losses, and to present it as though it settled the matter is to confuse a hypothetical with a policy. Where governments have tried to pay, the record is unimpressive, though the reasons are instructive. Programmes reserved for workers who could prove that their jobs were lost to imports required them to establish a cause that is often impossible to isolate, since a plant may close because of foreign competition, new machinery and poor management all at once. Many eligible workers never applied; many who applied were retrained for occupations that were themselves shrinking. The failure lay less in the idea of compensation than in tying it to a cause that could not be reliably identified. This suggests that the better course is not a trade-specific remedy at all but support that follows the worker regardless of why the job disappeared: insurance against lost earnings, help with moving to where work exists, and training linked to employers who are actually hiring. Such measures cannot be justified as payment for trade alone, and they will cost more than narrow programmes did. Yet the case for open trade has always rested on the claim that its benefits are broadly shared. If that claim is to be more than an assertion, the sharing has to be done by someone, and it will not happen by itself.
R05-F-06: Trade statistics were designed for a world in which goods were made in one place and sold in another. A customs officer records the full value of a shipment as it crosses the border and attributes it to the country from which it was sent. When a product is made from start to finish in a single country, this convention is harmless. When it is assembled from parts made in a dozen, the convention produces a curious distortion: the country where the last screw is turned is credited with the entire value of the product, including the much larger share that was created elsewhere and merely passed through. Consider a hypothetical tablet computer assembled in one country from a display made in a second, chips designed in a third and fabricated in a fourth, and software written in a fifth. When the finished tablet is shipped to a sixth country, the statistics record an export of its full factory price from the assembling country, though the work done there may account for only a small fraction of that price. The bilateral balance between the assembler and the buyer swells accordingly, while the suppliers of the costlier components, whose contribution travels unseen inside the assembler's shipment, appear in the bilateral figures as having sold nothing to the final market at all. Statisticians have responded by trying to trace value added: to ask, for each product, how much of its value was created in each country, and to tally trade on that basis. The striking feature of the results is not that a country's overall position changes, for it largely does not. Its balance with the world as a whole is much the same however one counts, since the value of each imported component is recorded once as an import and again inside the export, and the two entries cancel. What changes is the map: the bilateral balances that attract political attention are redistributed, often substantially, from assemblers towards the countries that supply the most valuable parts. This matters because bilateral balances are routinely read as a scorecard of who is gaining at whose expense, and policy is sometimes made on that reading. A tariff aimed at the country with which a large deficit is recorded may, on the value-added view, fall chiefly on workers who contributed a modest share of what was bought, while leaving untouched the countries that contributed the most. The value-added figures are not beyond dispute. They depend on tables of who buys inputs from whom that are compiled infrequently and filled out with estimates, and they cannot replace the gross figures that customs administrations need for their own purposes. But one need not regard them as precise to see that they expose a habit of reading the gross bilateral figures as though they measured something they were never built to measure.
R05-F-07: The argument for protecting infant industries is older than most of the arguments now made against it, and it is more respectable than its critics often allow. Its premise is that productivity in many industries is learned rather than given. A new steelworks or shipyard in a country without one begins with inexperienced workers, untested managers and suppliers who do not yet know what it needs; it will make costly mistakes for years before it reaches the efficiency of established foreign rivals. If it must meet those rivals at once, it may never survive long enough to learn. A period of protection, on this view, is not a subsidy to inefficiency but an investment in the learning that will eventually remove it. The argument gains force from a further point. Much of what a pioneering firm learns does not stay inside it. Workers it trains move to competitors, suppliers it develops go on to serve other customers, and the mere demonstration that an industry can work in a given place lowers the risk for those who follow. Over time a cluster of related firms may form around the pioneer, each drawing on skills that the pioneer paid to create. Because the pioneer bears the cost of this learning but captures only part of its benefit, an unaided market will produce too little of it, and there is a case in principle for public support. The difficulty lies not in the logic but in the ending. Protection is granted on the promise that it is temporary, yet every year it lasts it builds a constituency for its continuation: owners whose profits depend on it, workers whose jobs appear to, and officials whose standing is tied to the industry's survival. Worse, the protection itself weakens the motive to learn. A firm that knows its shelter will be extended whenever it fails to become competitive has little reason to bear the pain of becoming so, and the infant can remain an infant indefinitely, growing larger without growing up. The many cases in which protection outlived any plausible learning period are not accidents of bad administration; they are what the incentives predict. It follows that the argument stands or falls on whether the exit can be made credible in advance. Protection whose duration is fixed and public, whose renewal depends on measurable progress, and whose beneficiaries are required to compete in some market where the shelter does not reach them, such as export markets, is a different policy from protection granted open-endedly. Export performance is especially revealing, because a firm cannot fake competitiveness in a market it does not control. A protected firm that must also sell abroad, at prices set by rivals it cannot shut out, learns quickly whether it has improved, and so does the government that shelters it. The interesting historical question is therefore not whether successful industrialisers protected their industries, since many did, but whether they attached conditions that forced the protected firms to improve. None of this makes the conditions easy to impose. Withdrawing support from a large employer that has missed its targets requires a government able to bear the political cost, and the very constituency that protection creates is what makes that cost high. Protection also has victims who are easy to overlook: the firms that must buy the sheltered product at a higher price, and whose own competitiveness suffers as a result. The infant-industry case, then, is best understood not as a general licence but as a demanding bargain, sound in theory and available in practice only to states that can enforce its terms.
R05-F-08: The most familiar objection to industrial policy is that governments cannot pick winners. Officials, the objection runs, have neither the information nor the incentives to know which industries will flourish; investors risking their own money are better placed to judge, and when the state substitutes its judgement for theirs it will usually back the wrong horses and keep feeding them long after the race is lost. The objection has history on its side, in the sense that the record of state-backed ventures includes many expensive failures. But it rests on a picture of the problem that deserves closer inspection. The picture is one in which the menu of possible industries is known and the only question is which item to choose. Investors, in this picture, already know what a country could produce profitably, and the government's error is to overrule them. Yet for an economy trying to move into activities it has never undertaken, no one possesses this knowledge. Whether a particular region can grow cut flowers for export, assemble electronic components or write software for foreign clients depends on a mass of local particulars, from the reliability of the roads to the habits of the workforce, that can be learned only by trying. An investor asked in advance would have no better basis for a forecast than an official; both would be guessing. The relevant knowledge is not hidden in investors' heads waiting to be consulted; it does not yet exist. Producing it is costly, and here the market's usual advantages turn against it. The first entrepreneur to discover that a product can be made profitably in a given place bears the full cost of the experiment if it fails, but if it succeeds, others can copy the discovery cheaply, entering the industry once its viability has been shown. The pioneer thus bears the losses of failure while sharing the rewards of success, and rational investors will undertake fewer such experiments than the economy as a whole would want. The case for public involvement follows not from officials knowing more than investors, but from no one knowing enough and the cost of finding out being borne unevenly. If this is right, the objection about picking winners is aimed at the wrong target. A policy of supporting discovery will back many ventures that fail; that is what experiment means, and a programme that never failed would be one that was taking no risks. Measured by the share of its bets that pay off, a sound programme of discovery may look worse than a timid one. The genuine danger lies elsewhere: support, once given, may become impossible to withdraw, so that the losers are kept alive at public expense. What matters is less the ability to pick winners than the ability to let losers go, and the second ability, though rarely discussed, is at least as hard to acquire as the first. The approach has a cost of its own, and it would be dishonest to minimise it. Discovering what local firms could do requires officials to work closely with them, to learn what obstacles they face and what help would remove them. The same closeness that yields information also invites capture, in which those meant to be overseen come to set the terms. Officials who meet the same managers every month will find it hard to tell them, when a review date arrives, that support is ending. There is no formula that separates collaboration from collusion, only practices, such as public criteria and fixed review dates, that make the difference easier to see. That is a weaker guarantee than the advocates of industrial policy would like, but it is a stronger one than its critics usually assume.
